I). MONK (Jacques Cartier), Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I would like to call my right liou. friend's attention to the division of St. James, Montreal. My right hon. friend will remember that very nearly a month ago I called his attention to the fact that that division had not been represented at all during this long session of parliament. My right hon. friend stated at that time that he was under the impression that although his attention had been called to that matter some time previously by myself, still an agreement had been come to between us, or some statement had been made by myself, to the effect that the matter should rest there. This I denied at tiie time : hut my right hon. friend stated that the matter would be seen to at once. I would like to have from my right hon. friend an explanation of why the writ was not issued at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I am bound to say, first of all, in justice to my hon. friend, that when he called my attention to the matter, I made the statement which he has just repeated as having come from me, and which I made in perfect good faith at the time ; hut as I found no confirmation of it in ' Hansard ' I have to admit that

so far as that goes 1 was mistaken, and I beg my hon. friend to accept my apology for that. * With regard to the other question, the writ has not been issued for this reason. When our attention was called to the matter a few months ago-this session has been so long that it is almost impossible to keep track of time-we found that the lists in the city of Montreal were being prepared. My hon. friend knows that the disposition of the law is that the lists cannot come into force to be made use of in an election until sixty days have elapsed after they have been prepared. Therefore, it has been only within some few weeks at most that the writ could have been issued for the electoral division of St. James.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: Will my right hou. friend allow me to state that the lists came into force on the 11th day of May. They were revised in March.
I think the lists were prepared in May.
They were prepared in March, and came into force in May.

At all events, that is the reason. We did not think it would be useful, nor do I think my hon. friend was particularly anxious to have the writ issued until the session was over, and until, without any inconvenience to anybody, we could dispose of the business in hand, so that we could go to the country, in that particular division, fresh from the questions we have been discussing.

My right hon. friend is remarkably considerate. He changes his attitude with regard to the St. James division every time he mentions it in the House. Some six or eight weeks ago he distinctly took the ground that he was waiting for my hon. friend front Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) to bring the matter up. It seems remarkable that a constituency should stand unrepresented in this House for months because some member of the opposition did not force the government to issue a writ. However, my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier pointed out that there was nothing in that, because he had brought this matter to the attention of the government as soon as the constituency had been declared vacant. That was not two or three months ago ; it was something like six months ago, if I am not mistaken. Months rolled on and no action was taken. During all that time it would have been perfectly competent for the government to bring on the election, as the lists were all ready. The lists in the province of Quebec, so far as I understand the law, were revised in March last, and sixty days afterwords they would be ready for an election. On the 11th of May, as my hon. friend 419
from Jacques Cartier informs me, the lists were ready for an election in St. James' division, Montreal. The months of May, June, July, August and September elapsed, and we are now in the month of October ; and during all these weary months of this session that constituency has been unrepresented. I do not think the reasons which my right hon. friend has given for disfranchising the constituency during what amounts to an entire year are at all adequate. It would have been perfectly possible to have had a member for that constituency elected during the month of June last, and he would have been present in the House during the past four months to represent the people of that very important division. I am informed that not only were the lists ready, but they were printed in the Printing Bureau in May or June last, and that twenty copies were sent to the candidates who had last contested that division. Under these circumstances, we should surely have some better explanation than the right hon. gentleman has given us why that very important section of the city of Montreal has been unrepresented in parliament during so many months.

I understand the right hon. gentleman to say that the reason why the writ was not issued was that the lists of this year for St. James' division were not completed. I am glad to hear him take that stand, because, in the face of that there cannot be much truth in the rumour which is going about that we are soon to have a general election. The lists in the province of Ontario in many cases are not completed until the last days of December, so that we could not have an election before some time in March. So that the statement of the right hon. gentleman will please the politicians throughout the Dominion, as it means that we cannot possibly have a general election before March next.

Although, as you have been reminded by my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan), we have been here for something like seven months, still I think that the importance of the question of defence is so great and the estimates for that purpose which are being asked this year are so considerable, that it is proper we should take up a short time at least in discussing the present position of our militia force, and the intentions of the government with regard to it. The two items 29 and 30, more especially item 30 will cover the ground upon which I propose to speak. I think it will be more convenient that the general question should be discussed in a single statement rather than divide it up into the different heads suggested by the items in the estimates. The objects for which the militia force was established were first to aid the civil power, to maintain order, and in the second place to repel invasion or attack from without. The militia is the force of Canada upon which the government rely for assistance in maintaining order, in carrying.out the laws of the country, and in maintaining the integrity of our Dominion, if attacked or threatened. These are the purposes for which the militia force was originally established. These are the

Does that include the cost of the South African war ?

Yes, this covers every dollar of expenditure, direct and ordinary, for the militia, including the expenditure on the Fenian raid, the North-west rebellion and the South African war. It also includes the expense of maintaining the garrison at Halifax. It will be seen that the estimated expenditure for this year, including expenditures upon public buildings for the militia, amount to 68 cents per head of the population of Canada.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: That includes an expenditure of $1,200,000 on capital account?

Yes, for the current year. I find that the expenditure for this year, 68 cents per head, has been exceeded only twice since confederation, viz. In the year 1900, when it was 70 cents per head-this, of course, including the expense of the South African contingents-and in 1886, when it was 92 cents per head, this being the year during which nearly the whole of the expenditure in connection with the North-west rebellion was made, when the expenditure for the year on ordinary account, including the North-west rebellion, amounted to $4,055,000. I thought that these figures would be interesting, and would enable us. perhaps, to see exactly where we are with reference to the expenditure which this country is malting in connection with military matters. From my point of view, it is very gratifying to find that we have made this increase, that we are getting nearer to what I believe, and what I think the best citizens of the country believe, is our duty with reference to military matters and questions of defence. How much further we may be prepared to go, I cannot say. But I feel sure of this, that this parliament and this country will be ready to support the government in expenditures of this kind, so long as those expenditures are wise, and the development of the militia is carried on under wise rules and proper directions.
Now, I propose to discuss for a moment the expenditures which are now before the committee. I shall not now speak of the expenditures on account of public works for militia purposes, because these matters have already been discussed in the committee, when the estimates of the Minister of Public Works were under consideration. The expenditures are divided into ordinary
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
and capital, and that division, I think is obviously correct. The ordinary expenditure, of course, should be taken out of consolidated revenue, as it is the expenditure for the ordinary maintenance of the militia. The capital expenditure is special. It is chiefly for new armament, to some extent for rifle ranges, and, perhaps, the acquisition of lands for military purposes. This particular vote of $1,300,000 will be chiefly for the purpose of purchasing arms and ordnance and for purchasing equipment and clothing as a reserve. At the present moment we are inadequately armed. There are less than 40,000 rifles in this country whereas we need at least 100,000, and I believe we should have many more than that in reserve. Our field artillery is inadequately armed ; we should exchange the present guns for up-to-date weapons. Our garrison artillery is inadequately armed ; in many cases the armament is absolutely worthless and useless. That should be changed and we propose to change it.
I may be asked : Is $1,300,000 going to do all this ? Certainly not, but it is going to make a commencement. I may be asked -and it would be a fair question-what appropriations do you propose to ask in the future ; what is your policy with reference to expenditure on capital account ? I propose to anticipate this question. I have no hesitation in saying'that I think this vote will have to be repeated four or five times in order to place the militia in a proper and safe position particularly with respect to armament. When we come to vote the various items I will be able to state to the committee, at. least approximately, the disposition which it is proposed to make of the money.
Do I understand that this present estimate covers an additional arsenal ?

No, it does not. It includes an amount of $75,000 for reserve ammunition.
As I said a moment ago, I believe that the people of the country and this committee, while willing to give money freely for the benefit of the militia force, will be anxious as to its expenditure and will justify the granting of considerable sums such as we are asking only after being satisfied that the plan of expenditure is the wisest that could be adopted. This I think is the proper moment for explaining in a general way the scheme which we have in mind. One or two sessions ago I stated to the House that I looked forward to having in the near future a force of 100,000 men in Canada which might be called upon at any time and which would be ready within a brief period whenever its services might be required. I am happy to say that reflection and the experience of the last year or two lead me to believe more strongly than ever that such a force can be counted upon and

that it can be counted upon without very much increase i;n the expend!(hire on consolidated revenue account. The scheme briefly and roughly outlined is this: That we shall proceed as we are doing now with an enlistment of say 40,000 or 50,000 of this 100,000 men, this enlistment to be called a peace establishment. Of that 40,000 or 45,000 probably at least fifty per cent, that is twenty-five per cent of the whole 100,000 of the establishment, shall be asked to do annual drill; that all the officers and non-commissioned officers for the total force of 100,000 men shall be required to do annual drill, and that the twenty-five per cent or less of the 100,000 men, say, 22,000 men who will be required to do annual drill, shall be selected men, men who will represent-if I am not making use of a term that is objectionable to some of my friends-the skeleton of the force of 100,000 men.
In connection with a force of this kind it will be absolutely necessary that you should have all the departments of an army properly represented. You cannot put an army into the field unless you have the means of supplying them with food, clothing, arms, transportation and everything that is necessary for their comfort in the field, and in order to do that you must have permanently established in time of peace all the departments which you would require in time of war. This is an essential not only at headquarters but in every one of the whole twelve military districts of the Dominion. We now have too, in this country, I am happy to say, an efficient permanent force, perhaps not as efficient as it ought to be, but a force which has done, and is doing excellent work. This force was created for the purpose of educating the active militia; It supplies the teaching power from which the officers who will have charge of this force of 100,000 men and also the non-commissioned officers and the selected men will get their training. Every man who reflects will realize that the most important point in order to bring about an efficient military force is to have the leaders, whether they be officers, non-commissoned officers, or selected men, thoroughly trained and ready for action at any moment. This is an important and vital part of our scheme. Then the question would be asked :	What
are you going to do with the other 60 per cent ? You have some 40 per cent enlisted for what you may call a peace footing, but where are the 60 per cent and where are you going to find them when you may require them for active service ? Our proposal in regard to the 60 per cent is that they shall be enlisted for the requirements in time of war, but that in the meantime they shall not be required to drill unless they choose to do so, but that they shall be taught the use of the rifle and shall be given rifles and ammunition to use at their homes or at convenient points, that they shall he enrolled so that when an emergency arises they can be brought in and incorporated with this 25 per cent which I have referred to, and which shall be the flesh and blood, so to speak, to be put on the skeleton which will go to make 'up the army. That is roughly an outline of the scheme. I may say, in passing, that we have done a good deal already towards looking after the 60 per cent, the 60,000 upon whom we have to call to make up our army to 100,000. We have already inaugurated a system of rifle associations. We require the men who join these rifle associations to sign a bond or agreement to serve if required in war. We are at present doing this and we are giving them an opportunity to learn the use of the rifle by giving to each association of forty the use of ten rifles. We have established first-class rifle ranges all over the country, and I am glad to say that we have something like 20,000 men now enrolled in these rifle associations. During the last four or five years we have constructed rifle ranges in nearly all of the important centres of Canada. We have in this city the Rockliffe Rifle Range, which is one of the best rifle ranges in the world. We have rifle ranges at London, Hamilton, Niagara, Toronto, Kingston, Montreal, Three Rivers, Sherbrooke, LSvis, St. John, N.B., Fredericton, Campbellton, Moncton, Bedford near Halifax and in British Columbia, and so I might go on.

In order to carry out tlie scheme of education and training which is the very groundwork of the efficiency of our militia force, it is proposed to establish a central camp at a convenient place in the interior, where all the officers of the force and certain representatives from every corps in Canada may he brought together, a ground large enough to enable military evolutions to he carried out to some extent as they would be in actual warfare, a camp ground which would probably embrace from 20,000 to 30,000 acres of land. To this central camp the permanent force would be brought, and there the plan of education which 1 have outlined and upon the importance of which I cannot too much insist, would be carried out in the best possible manner. It is not proposed to give up district camps. On the contrary, it is hoped that we shall be able to extend the ground for the camps in the different districts so that the officers and non-commissioned officers who have learned their work at this central school will be able to return to their own districts, and there have an opportunity of teaching the men with who-m they are more immediately associated. It is intended I may say in this connection, to increase the number of mounted men. They should at least be trebled and probably quadrupled. There are certain districts of this country, the eastern townships, points along the frontier in different parts of Ontario, and in the North-west especially, where this force can be easily enlisted, and where you can get a class of men who will go into the cavalry who would not think of joining the infantry. It is proposed to utilize these men in this way.
Now, perhaps, this would be as convenient a moment as any to discuss the question of the pay of the militia. I have read some reports in the newspapers and I have heard some statements in this House as to the views of some of my hon. friends connected with the militia upon this question. This is not the first time it has been discussed. Some comparisons have been made between the city and rural militia. The city militia have been changed with the expenditure on their magnificent drill halls and armouries and we have been told that the rural militia have nothing to place against these. This was done, X think, in a debate to justify the argument that we should pay the rural militia a dollar a day and keep the pay of the city militia at the same rate. It was pointed out by my hon. friend that it was true the city militia gave every cent of their pay into a common fund.
Most of them.

Yet, notwithstanding that, it was argued that, in view of the splendid accommodation they got and of the fact that they had their drill at night, which did not interfere with their days work, we should discriminate by increasing the pay of the rural militia without increasing the pay of the city militia. I dissent from that view. I think we must treat all alike. While the city militia may have some advantages in the respects I have mentioned, they do give up their pay, they are always on hand, and are the first to be called upon in the case of any trouble.

Eet me say one word of explanation. I urged very strongly that the pay of all the militia, including the city, should be increased, but that if the funds were not sufficient, then the increase should apply to the rural corps for the reasons I gave on that occasion.
that will foster military ardour and encourage our young men to join the militia and complete their term of service, and I propose that encouragement should be given in the shape of a reward to those who have done continuous and faithful service.
The question of the p>ay of our permanent force has been mentioned, and I was to day asked a question with reference to it. I can only say that the position of the permanent force has been enormously improved within the past three years. A pension law has been passed, under which every man who serves in the permanent force will be taken care of in his old age. Formerly men who had served until they had become too old, men who had done good work and had risen to the rank of sergeant or sergeant-major had to retire without any pension. I have a case this very year, in which I am asking parliament to give a gratuity to a sergeant-major, who served the best of his days in the permanent force, who had gone beyond the age limit, and hadi to retire without any allowance. Thank heaven that disgraceful state of things is at an end; and now our permanent force men will be getting something more than forty cents a day and their clothing, lodging, rations, &c. If they are faithful i to their duty and remain in the corps, they are certain of being taken care of, in some sort at any rate, in their old age. I would also like to point this out to the men of the permanent force, if they are sufficiently interested to read what I am saying. It is I open to any man in our permanent force to rise to the highest position in the militia. I am happy to say that we have to-day officers in the force who' began their military career i as privates in the permanent force of this country.
Can the hon. minister give us a few names ?

I do not see how we could discriminate. I wish to point out further to my hon. friend that the rural battalions are provided with tents and transportation and are fed, and I do not think it is fair to charge against the city battalions some of the extravagant expenditures of which both the late and the present government have been guilty, in the erection of armouries, which are altogether more expensive than were necessary. I do not know that I should go any further into this question of pay except to say this, that I am looking carefully into the subject and feel disposed to go upon the lines to which I have referred. I feel disposed to ask that increased pay be granted for good conduct to men who turn out regularly and show an intelligent and earnest interest in the force. One of our great troubles-and I am sure it would be just as great if it were a dollar a day-is that a man will attend one annual drill and then get a good job and you will never see him again. I want to do something if possible

speechtext: I could give one or two, but I do not think it worth while.

Are there a number of non-commissioned officers who have served in the regular army and are now employed in the permanent corps ?

I think there are. I would apply the principle in. existence now in the Northwest Mounted Police. Have a rate of pay for the first year and increase it every year of good service up to a proper point. That is the reform I would propose in connection with the permanent force. But, Sir, we have not only to consider the men.^ but we have to consider the non-commissioned officers and officers. I am prepared to admit at once that the pay of the non-commis-

sioned officers is insufficient and should be increased, and must be increased. And the same is true with regard to the officers. We should give the officers at least as good pay as is given in the British army. I think we should give them better pay. That is a matter to be considered. But here, again, let me point out what has been done for the officers as well as for the non-commissioned officers and privates of thei permanent force. We have established a pension law. It is true, we call upon the officers to contribute. They contribute five per cent of their pay. But upon retiring they get a most generous pension. And not only this, but if anything happens to them, if they are killed or die, their widows and their children are taken care of. So our officers of the permanent force are very much better treated than they were before.
I am sorry to find I am occupying so much time-I thought I should finish in half an hour. But I wish to proceed upon the line I have just mentioned and devote a short time to pointing out what has been done in the way of improving the condition of the militia, and what is about to be done. I will only name some of the changes which have been made. I have already mentioned the pension law. Let me refer to the limitation of the term of commission. Let me refer to the establishment of the reserve of officers. That was being done, I think, by my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) my predecessor, about the time I came in. It had been arranged for, but I am happy to say that I have had the satisfaction of carrying it into force and1 insisting on its being done.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman is not now referring to the permanent force 1

No, but to the whole militia. The term of an officer in command of the militia to-day is limited to five years. When I came into office there were about fifty colonels who had been serving forty years more or less giving no opportunity whatever for a young man to rise, and taking away every inducement almost for a young man to enter the militia force at all. Now we have the enforcement of the age limit. We had colonels away beyond the age limit, we had captains away beyond the age limit, we had nra'ors away beyond the age limit, and lieutenants-why I myself knew some lieutenants who were over sixty. It is now possible for us to get rid. of these well-meaning gentlemen who, no doubt, have served their country very faithfully. The lieutenant who was sixty had no opportunity to rise, because his colonel, who was seventy, had been in command for thirty or forty years, and the major, who was sixty, had held his place for about as long. Of course, I am not finding fault, but simply pointing out the fact that this was the condition of things which actually existed and which, I Sir F. W. BORDEN.
am happy to say, has been absolutely changed, so that, to-day we have, as a result of these promotions, given the younger officers who enter the force the reasonable hope that, within eight or ten years they will be occupying high positions in their regiments if they deserve it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Might I ask a question ? Is that change necessarily in the interest of the militia ? It is since that change was made that we find the complaints that we have only the skeleton of a militia turning out. May not this have been a detriment to the force.' ?

speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND. DEFENCE.

speechtext: I understand that the term of office for a colonel is limited to five years ?

Yes, but there is a regulation by which, upon the recommendation of the district officer commanding and the further recommendation of the general, the tenure of office may be extended by one, two, or three years, the limit being three years. It may happen that there is no major-the second in command-qualified to take the colonel's place. And it may be in the interest of the force-and it must be shown to be in the interest of the force-to extend the term of command for not more than four years.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Military qualifications to be the only requisite ?

The only requisite, so far as I know. Another reform effected under the present regime is to insist upon annual camps. We have had annual camps ever since 1896. In my opening remarks I spoke of the importance of an army having all the departments of a working force actually in existence in time of peace, and doing in time of peace the work that they wopld be required to do in lane of war.
In this connection, we have inaugurated a system of medical service under the supervision first of Colonel Neil-

son, and now under Lieutenant-Colonel Fiset, who distinguished) himself so greatly at Paardeburg. We have organized bearer companies. There was not one in Canada before. We have field hospitals. There was not one in Canada before. Wei have an army medical staff, which did not exist.
We have organized an intelligence branch of the service which did not exist before, for the purpose, as the committee knows, of collecting the information that might be necessary for the commanding officers to use in time of war. In connection with the intelligence branch, surveys are being made of the thickly-settled parts of the country, and I hope to be able, to get the necessary funds to make an accurate military survey of the country, which will be most useful. This is a thing that is done in every other country. I hope to see maps prepared and placed on sale in the book-stores, which will be of immense benefit to the people of the country and to people visiting this country.
We have organized an army service corps which previously did not exist. This is under the supervision of Lieutenant Colonel Biggar, who had service in this connection in South Africa which has been of great advantage to him and who has taken a special course at Aldershot to fit him for the position. I believe he is a most efficient officer. In connection with the army service corps, instructions are being given in every military district, lectures are given before the camps and a small permanent staff has been established.
Then we have the ordnance branch, which is now being created for the first time in Canada. This is, of course, very largely the old stores' branch of the Militia Department, which has been under the direct control of the minister. For years and years, certainly for the last ten years, a change in this respect has been advocated. It was altogether an anomalous condition that the stores, rifles and articles of that kind should be under the control of the civil head of the department. I had not been very long in my position when I was impressed with the force of that statement. We have now adopted the English system ; we are creating an ordnance branch, and have appointed Colonel Macdonald, the very able and worthy head of the old stores' branch, to the important post of head of the ordnance branch, placing him under the supervision of the general officer commanding. As under the British system, he is still under the control of the minister, but he is under the supervision of the general officer commanding.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Does that cover all the stores ?
That covers everything.
speakername: Tlie MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: But he does not buy them ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I understood the minister to say that the ordnance branch is under the supervision of the general officer commanding as well as of the hon. minister himself.

We have adopted the phraseology of the English Order in Council, which says that certain departments shall be under the control of the general officer commanding and that certain others shall be under his supervision.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: In case of a conflict with respect to the management of this department between the general officer commanding and the minister, what would occur ?

That is a case that would scarcely arise. The Order in Council provides that the minister, if he chooses, may consult the head of a great department such as the ordnance department, the administration of which involves great expenditures of money and important questions of policy. In the English service this applies to the quartermaster general as well, and to one or two other similar positions in the War Office.
I think it is convenient to follow, as far as possible, the course of the War Office in this, because it is desirable that our organization here should be as nearly as possible like that of the War Office.
We have also established an engineering branch, and I have been able to secure as the chief of the branch Major Weatherbee. a graduate of the Royal Military College at Kingston. Mr. Weatherbee has just returned after having taken a long course in England to fit him for this position. He has as his assistant Captain Maunsell, whom I found in the service, who was appointed by the hon. ex-minister (Hon. Mr. Tisdale), and is one of the most efficient officers in the service.

I omitted to refer to the engineer branch of the pei'manent force. As we have made the ordnance a branch of the permanent force, and all the employees, soldiers of the permanent force and \inder military control ; so we propose to have in every military district, or rather as a part of every military depot of the permanent force, a small section of engineers. There is no engineer force to-day in the permanent militia force at all. We have a few scattered companies of engineers. It is a most important thing to have an up-to-date, educated and thoroughly trained engineer force, and we want a section of it in every one of the depots in the Dominion. The strength of this force will be about 100 ; so that we will have 100 ordnance corps, 100 engineer corps, 200 Montreal depot, and 100 Strathcona Horse, making in all 500. I cannot hope to have all of these established during the present year, but the ordnance corps and the engineer corps, and I hope the Strathcona Horse will be established within a very short time.
Now, Sir, I wish for a moment to speak of the state of the militia generally. Notwithstanding the criticisms which have been vouchsafed against the militia, and notwithstanding the failures, perhaps lamentable failures in some respects, I believe that as a whole, as a going concern, as a machine fit to do work if called upon ; the militia force is in fairly good condition to-day. I think that was pretty amply proven two or three years ago in the despatch of the contingents to South Africa ; in the preparation within a fortnight of a force of one thousand men scattered over 2,000 or 3,000 miles of territory ; and in the despatch later on, of artillery and cavalry within a space of perhaps three weeks. All this has shown that there is some vitality in the Canadian militia, and some power to do its work, notwithstanding that some of the camps have seemed to be lamentably small. I maintain that as a going concern the militia is in a far better shape than it was ever before, and is in a fairly satisfactory condition. But much more can be done ; much more must be done, and it must 'chiefly be done in the line of educating and training the leaders of this force. This is the direction in which I think we should chiefly expend our money. If we had an unlimited amount of money to train 100,000 men, I daresay it would be a better proposition to call them all out and spend our money, and have the force up to date in every particular. But we cannot do that. It is a question of doing the best we can with the money we have, and I think the amount of money we are asking from the people for the militia this year, is perhaps pretty near the top of what we should ask in the near future. If that be so, we must be content with perfecting the different departments of the militia ; we must be content with affording the very best possible means for the education of the officers, non-commissioned officers and selected men ; we must be content with supplying the sixty per cent whom we are not asking to turn out to drill, with rifles, with ammunition, with targets, with instructions in the art of shooting.
But I think that the idea which I have put forward-which is Lord Dun-donald's idea, which is the idea his predecessor approved of-of having turned out annually to drill, all the officers and noncommissioned officers, and a skeleton of the men ; I believe that this means you will get a fairly effective skeleton upon which you can put the plastic material, the flesh and blood, out of which you could make an army. Some one has alluded to the shadow of a skeleton. Well, I beg to dissent from that view. It would have been more correct to have said a skeleton from which some of the smaller bones are absent-and a good many of the small bones seem to have been absent in one or two of the military districts in the western

part of Ontario. As to the flesh and blood, as to the plastic material, the 60 per c-ent that we propose to utilize to fill out this skeleton, and make it strong and stalwart and able to defend ; I can point with confidence to the evidence that has been given by the militia men of former days ; the men who engaged in repelling the Fenian invasion ; the men who engaged in putting down the two Northwest rebellions ; the men who volunteered for South Africa and won glory for their country ; the men who were second to none in heroism; the men who never turned their backs upon the foe
speakername: The MINISTER OP MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

I have unbounded confidence in the capacity of these men, if we give them an opportunity of learning how to use a rifle, that they will fill up the ranks, and provide the flesh and blood, the plastic material, that round out this skeleton and make an army fit for duty whenever it is required.
I have already referred to the importance of housing the militia. If we want to make the infantry force of this country what it ought to be, we must provide for every single unit, every company, sufficient accommodation for at least 100 men, where they may meet together and spend their evenings, using it as a sort of club-room, and having blackboards and other means to educate themselves in the art of war. If you do that, you will excite renewed interest among the men, and you will get together and get the sympathy of the very best men in the community. You will not then have to worry over the question whether you are to pay them 75 cents or a dollar or fifty cents a day. It is not the money that brings that class of men out. It is the loyal spirit in them, and the desire to serve their country ; and all they will ask is the opportunity to acquire the necessary knowledge in order to do so.
I would like to say one word with regard to the Royal Military College. This is an institution of which we are all justly proud. It has sent men to fill prominent places in the British army. I think there were something like a hundred officers, graduates of the Military College, taking part in the South African war ; and one or two of them greatly distinguished themselves there, and are to-day occupying in that country positions of very great responsibility. In 1896 the Royal Military College was almost in the throes of dissolution. There were scarcely a baker's dozen in the college. There were not) more than half a dozen graduates. To-day, instead of having to look around and ask for young men to come to the college, we have the agreeable fact staring us in the face that the young men have to compete to get into the college. Whereas formerly the classes were composed of ten or twelve .or less, to-day every place in the college is filled, and each year at the examination there are half a dozen or a dozen Sir F. W. BORDEN.
more young men who are anxious to get in. Only a day or two ago I had a letter from a gentleman in Canada whose son has a commission in the British army, in which he sent me a quotation from a letter which he had just received from his son telling him in what high estimation this college was held in England and in the British army ; and well it might be.
I am happy to be able to say that whereas during the early years of my administration we could hardly induce a graduate of the college to pome into our force, to-day we have a considerable number of graduates in the permanent force of this country. This is because they see that the force, fo same extent at least, is being cared for, and that there is some future for it, and also because we have provided a generous pension fund which will insure the care of the men after they have passed the years prescribed as the limit of military age. We have to-day in the intelligence branch three or four graduates of the Royal Military College, which is most satisfactory to me. It is all very well, and we cannot regret very much, perhaps, to see our young men going into the British army and taking prominent places there ; but I must say I would very much prefer seeing them remain at home and endeavour to work out the problems which we have to solve in this country, the solution of which need their assistance.
I wish to refer to the recent establishment of a rifle factory in this country. I think lion, gentlemen will all agree with me that it is important that the militia force of this country should be as far as possible a self-contained as well as a self-reliant force, and that we should be able to manufacture our own rifles as we are manufacturing our own ammunition. Our rifle is not precisely the same as the service rifle in England ; but there is practically no difference, while the ammunition used is exactly the same. So that if a British force were fighting alongside of ours, or vice versa, no difficulty could possibly arise from the fact of their using two slightly different rifles.
Then, as I have stated, we have enlarged our arsenal. Formerly the cartridge factory at Quebec was turning out in the whole year as many cartridges as the Woolwich arsenal was turning out in one day. Today we are able to turn out, or will he before this year is through, 13,000,000 rounds of cartridges, as against 1,500,000 seven years ago. We have established, in connection with the arsenal, a school of gunnery. We are not only making cartridges for rifles, but*we have put in the necessary plant to make shells and all the projectiles required for the use of larger guns, and we are con- ' structing a building at a cost of some $30,000 for the purpose of a Dominion school of gunnery.
We are devoting more attention also, as far as we can under the present

condition of the law, to the encouragement of cadets. I am sorry that we are not able to do more ; but we are prescribing systems of instruction, and we are sending drill-sergeants whenever requested to do so, and to some of the older classes we have been able to supply rifles. This is only a beginning. I recognize in the cadets, the young lads at school and college, the material which will make up the future army of this country if it should ever be required for serious work. That is the time to make the impression on the young mind. Three or four weeks of drill and training at that time will do more good, I was going to say, than an equal number of years after a man has reached the age of twenty-five or thirty.
In this connection perhaps I may say a single word as to the militia law. Early in the session I gave notice that I would introduce a Militia Bill. A Bill was prepared, but I was asked later on, through the colonial office, if I would go to England and discuss certain changes which I had made up my mind to introduce ; and I might have gone if I had known that we were going to have such a long, interesting and pleasant session as this, and might have returned in time to introduce my Bill. But I did not know that and consequently thought better to leave the Bill over to another year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Does the hon. minister not think he will be able to bring it up yet this session ?

I shall consider that. I do not think it is desirable, perhaps, that I should go into the question of what I propose in the Bill, under the circumstances. When the time comes to introduce it it will be time enough to discuss its provisions. In conclusion, I have only to say that I hope the committee will not consider the programme which I have laid down as too ambitious. I believe it is a programme which can be carried out, and I have every confidence that if this or some similar line of action is proceeded with it will be possible for us to have within a measureable period-I would say five years at least-one of the best militia fighting organizations on the face of the earth.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Last year, when discussing militia matters, I used the following words, which I shall quote as expressing my feelings at present:
I shall make my remarks on this subject entirely free from politics, and entirely free from any fault finding, even if there be room for finding fault. It is my opinion, as I have often said before, that the militia should be kept entirely out of polities. It is above and beyond rail politics. Of course, it must to some extent have a political bearing because the minister who controls our militia for the time being must belong to one or other of the political parties, but so far as I am concerned I will exclude politics as much as possible from the consideration of this question. If I have any fault to
find with the Minister of Militia, or with the manner in which the contingents were despatched to South Africa, I propose to do as the Liberals do in the old country : viz., keep my criticism until the war is over and then bring the minister to account. I intend to show to the people of the world that whatever our politicai disagreements may be in Canada, we are ready and willing to show a united front in defence of our country and of the empire, and to leave complaint and criticism until we have conquered the enemy.
I do not propose to bring any politics into tile discussion to-day. At tlie same time, if I find it necessary or desirable to indulge in any criticism, I shall not be debarred from doing so through the fear that anybody would think I was moved by political reasons. I would just say one word about politics and then drop that subject altogether during this discussion. I want to warn my bon. friend the Minister of Militia that he will have to be very careful, very strong-minded and firm in order to keep politics out of this question. He will have to stiffen his backbone and make his will stronger if lie is going to do that effectively, because I think, in spite of the glowing picture he has given us of the state of the militia to-day, there are some difficulties which require to be remedied. I do not propose just now to take up the propositions of the hon. gentleman, because that can be better done at a later stage in the few remarks which I propose to make in connection "with this most important matter. We have had three very important events within the year, with which our military organization has some connection. We have had the South African difficulty ended, and we have had a Colonial Conference and a new Major General to take command of our forces. The South African peace having been accomplished, now is the time, as I said in my remarks last year, for criticism. Fortunately that war is over and we contemplate with pride and sorrow the louely graves which mark the valour and endurance of our young men who gave up their lives for the maintenance oftlie empire and the credit of Canada. Our heroes who survive have returned and taken off their war paraphernalia, and you would scarcely know them now from the other individuals gathered throughout our country, but, in common with their dead comrades, they will ever live in the hearts and memories of Canadians for the valour they displayed and the evidence they gave the world that Britain no longer stands alone, but is surrounded by her children, ever prepared, when the call is sufficiently urgent, to unite and uphold British unity and the glorious principles that underlie the British constitution. Before proceeding to discuss the Colonial Conference, I wish to make some reference to the militia report. I think we may congratulate ourselves upon our good fortune in getting so distinguished and gallant a soldier as our present Major General to take

command of the militia. He has been with us now sufficiently long to enable us to appreciate his work. Before coming here lie had some experience of the militia of Canada, because he is one of the ablest soldiers which the great empire found it necessary to send to South Africa. I propose to read some extracts from his report, so as to show where we stand in connection with those very important matters to which my bon. friend the Minister of Militia has alluded. In his report he says :
I have proposed that in future the regimental establishments of the active militia shall be at war strength, each unit containing in addition within itself the germ of a reserve. These proposals have met with your general approval, and I am now drawing up the establishments which, when complete, I will submit to you
1 may say that in his report he gives no explanation about the result, but my hon. friend has given us some insight into that. The Major General proceeds to say :
These camps of instruction covered a total period of twenty-five days, the whole of which I devoted to the personal supervision of the training, visiting each camp in turn.
As men who have only nine working days in the year to learn their duties as soldiers and non-commissioned officers cannot afford to spend any of that time on ceremonial, I arranged that instruction should be entirely devoted to practical work.
The officers and men under instruction worked with great zeal and intelligence, and though the system was in many cases quite new to them, they picked it up very quickly, and the tactical exercises engaged in towards the end of the training were useful in showing to all ranks how much they had still to learn before they could be considered efficient soldiers, let alone non-commissioned officers qualified to instruct and lead others.
Observation at these camps has shown me that the Canadian soldier takes the greatest interest in anything which his intelligence proves to him is of real practical benefit. Therefore, I propose in future to leave out marches past and ceremonial, ar.d instead to convert the camp3 practically into schools of instruction for fitting the soldier to take the field, with not one item in the programme that does not make for fighting efficiency. -
Though the rural militia contains a large proportion of earnest, self-sacrificing officers and men, it does not satisfy the requirements of a national defence force. Nominally it is a body of men who engage to serve for a period cf three years. As a matter of fact it consists and always has consisted of a number of regiments which are almost recruited afresh every time they are called out for training. Large numbers of entirely raw men enlist before the particular training and are perhaps never seen afterwards, no real effort being made to compel them to fulfil their engagement, owing to powers of compulsion being quite inadequate for the purpose. Consequently it is impossible to carry instruction beyond the most elementary stages. Such a system is unduly expensive and ineffective from a military point of view. So small is the rate of pay, and so unsatisfactory have been the conditions of training, that the best men do not enter the militia as they might. From this it follows that the non-commissioned officers also 1 are to a large extent insufficiently qualified for j their posts, nor can they command ready Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
obedience from the soldier when, as in many cases, they are quite ignorant of the very rudiments of their duties. Numbers of men go out to camp as non-commissdoned officers without any previous training whatever, and the proportion of these men who are new to the rank on such occasions shows clearly that there is a want of continuity in the personnel of the units.
As with some of the non-commissioned officers, so it is with some of the officers. Many have evidently not studied their profession sufficiently to act as the leaders and instructors of their non-commissioned officers and men. I make suggestions, later, on this matter.
Self-instruction by means of books, lectures to their men in well-appointed comfortable armouries (when these are provided) during the winter, and thoroughly practical work in the summer months will, joined with the excellent spirit which pervades the officer class of the Canadian militia, soon, I anticipate, produce the required result.
Material.
There is a great deficiency of all kinds of military stores and material essential for active service. This deficiency should be made good in time of peace.
It is absolutely necessary that the regulation allowance of every article of equipment required for mobilization of companies should be at company headquarters, for regimental mobilization at regimental headquarters.
Though there appears to be almost a sufficient stock of camp equipment for the existing units at their present strength, there is certainly no reserve available for the large force which would have to be placed in the field in time of war.
City Corps.
The city regiments, under the present organization would as a whole be the easiest to mobilize. but even they cannot in any sense be said to approach a state of readiness to take the field. They labour under the greatest difficulties and disadvantages. They all suffer from want of field training, owing to the fact that they get practically no camp experience. The allowances for instruction are too small ; so, in the rr ost efficient of the corps much of the necessary expense has to be undertaken by the officers and men instead of by the public. This unfair expense causes the loss of many good officers to the country. Many corps suffer from want of proper accommodation in the way of armouries, &e. Deficiencies of this kind have either to be made up by private effort or the corps must suffer.
Army Service Corps.
This branch of the service has been started I his year. Of the four skeleton companies authorized, two are now complete and another is in process of organization. Lieutenant Colonel Biggar and two non-commissioned officers were sent to Aldershot where they were given every advantage by the authorities to gain information on artmy service corps work.
Since his return to Canada. Lieutenant Colonel Biggar has conducted a six weeks' course of instruction at Montreal with the company there, with satisfactory results	[DOT]
He goes on to speak very highly of the school of musketry, and I think I will read part of that, because I consider that one of the most important improvements that have been made :
.	School of Musketry.
Courses of instruction were held during the months of July and August at the Roekliffe Rifle

Range. The number of officers and non-commissioned officers taking the course totalled sixty, this being double the number that attended the same term ot the previous year. Of these 31 officers and 22 non-commissioned officers obtained certificates.
Under the able and energetic command of Lieutenant Colonel Cartwright, the inspector of musketry and commandant of the School of Musketry, great progress has been made in the past year in extending and popularizing the knowledge of rifle shooting throughout Canada. The history of the new rifle clubs shows a steady growth, and the value of the work done by the School of Musketry, not in the teaching of shooting, but in the teaching of instructors in shooting can hardly be overestimated, even though its work is as yet on a small scale
I read these things, not merely for the information of the House, but to get them on ' Hansard,' where they can be seen by the country. Because we get too little out of this report. A number of military gentlemen get it, but the country generally seem to get very little knowledege of it. He speaks of the cavalry thus :
I have issued a memorandum on the training of the mounted troops of Canada, and also a new syllabus of instruction. I have assimilated the equipment and training of all branches of mounted troops.
I am preparing Instructions for the militia on their training, dealing in particular with musketry. field engineering and field work generally.
Referring to the cadet corps, he says :
This branch of the national defence system might easily be of the greatest value to the country, but from various causes it is at present of little account.
The results of the present system compare very unfavourably with what has been achieved in Australasia.
The whole cadet corps question requires to he considered and reorganized on workable lines, as the youth of the country are splendid material now lying waste from the military point of view.
Arrangements should be made to furnish every cadet corps of a certain strength with proper instruction.
These extracts give us knowledge not only of the condition of our militia, but of the capacity, industry and enthusiasm of the Major General Commanding. There is not a detail so small as to escape him, and there is no matter so difficult that he will not undertake its Improvement. I say again we have to congratulate ourselves that we have in command a man whose record and reputation we have every reason to be proud of, and not only that, but a man of straightforward common sense, a man of capacity and indefatigable industry. It will be the fault of the department and of the people of Canada if he does not make a success of the militia, and I prophecy that with the proper assistance he will do so to a very large extent. Now, let me read an extract or two in connection with the Colonial Conference, which shows to what extent the government committed this country on the question of defence. Here is an extract from 420
the report of the Canadian government to the Colonial Conference :
But while thus calling attention to the progress that has already been made by Canada In her militia organization, the ministers are far from claiming that perfection has been attained. If defects exist, there is every desire on the part of the Canadian government to remove them, and for this purpose the advice and assistance of experienced imperial officers will be welcomed and all reasonable efforts made to secure an efficient system.
In conclusion, the ministers repeat that, while the Canadian government are obliged to dissent from the measures proposed, they fully appreciate the obligation of the Dominion to make expenditures for the purposes of defence in proportion to the increasing population and wealth of the country. They are willing that these expenditures shall be so divested as to relieve the taxpayer of the mother country from some of the burdens which he now bears ; and they have the strongest desire to carry out their defence schemes in co-operation with the imperial authorities and under the advice of experienced Imperial officers so far as this is consistent with the principle of local self-government which has proved so great a factor in the promotion of imperial unity
At that time also we had some important information showing the expenditure per capita of the different colonies, including Canada, in connection with defence, showing that Canada had the lowest rate of expenditure, per capita, and only about one-fourteenth that of the mother country.
What did they give as the pei* capita expenditure of Canada ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Two shillings. That would be about the average up to this year, according to the figures given by the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence.
The MINISTER OF' MILITIA AND DEFENCE. Pretty nearly.

I will not trouble the House with these figures. My olij'ect was simply to show the position that our government took with regard to this matter. I think that in these militia matters we should support -any proposals emanating from the government unless we find in them something very wrong. If I find the government proceeding upon wrong principles, I am prepared to call attention to their errors. But the government represent ihe whole country for the time being, and they have committed the country, directly or indirectly, to the empire in regard to this matter. Therefore, I think both sides should support the government, except where the government is clearly and widely wrong ; and those who may not be quite satisfied can wait until they get into power to improve upon the government's proposals. I quite agree with the hon. member for Hal-dimand (Mr. Thompson) when he said :
Taking all these quotations together we find an absolute pledge given by our representatives for' militia betterment, a pledge given



on an occasion of grave importance, reduced to writing, mistake or misunderstanding an impossibility.
That brings us to the main question, the state of the militia at the present time and the proposals made by the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence for its betterment. I must say that his presentation of his request for increased expenditure and of his very broad and ambitious scheme for the improvement of the militia of Canada is of very great interest and requires a great deal of consideration. For my own part, 1 am prepared to join with parliament in approving of an expenditure even beyond what I might myself consider necessary if those in charge of the militia of this country considered it necessary for the advancement of our national defence. While this scheme is of such magnitude that it will startle some people, there is no question that if it is practicable and is properly and carefully carried out it will lay the foundation of a magnificent scheme of defence. On general lines I approve of the policy proposed, but, when X do so, it must be understood that we are not relying solely upon expenditure, and that this expenditure will be supplemented by successful work in other lines. If we are to have an effective system we must be prepared to face the expense, but my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence must not forget that, if we are to entrust him with this very large sum of money, the expenditure of that money must be supplemented by efficient instructions, work and results, so that we may have a proper and sufficient actual fighting force, supplemented with the same sort of reserve. Owing to the South African war and to other troubles which my hon. friend mentioned, he must remember that the expenditure on a peace footing has been very much less than the larger sum he now asks, as all of the present estimates for the militia are on a strictly peace footing, and I admired the courage and straightforwardness of the hon. minister when he said that we will have to stand this increased expenditure for three or four years.
Probably five years.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
My own opinion is that if we embark on this scheme and it can be made a success, it is probable that the annual grant required will never become less. I am not afraid of such an expenditure, especially if the country continues to make progress at its present rate. I believe that'if such an expenditure as this is worth while, we should undertake it at once and with our eyes open. With the great development of our industries, production and population, with the prominence that is given to great imperial and colonial - matters in the old country, I am most optimistic with regard to the future of this country for no country under Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
heaven to-day offers the inducements to the immigrant that Canada does. We have seen a great colonial minister resign from the highest place that the ambition of man can contemplate in order to fight the battle of closer union between the various portions of the British empire. That battle is of the utmost importance to Canada for when it is won we will have an illimitable market, a market for more than we can produce for scores of years to come, and we will have flowing to our shores all the immigration we desire, and the best immigrants in the world. I do not agree with my hon. friend from North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) wlio the other day said that we will in a few years to come ship wheat from Port Arthur into the United States because the population of that country will increase in that time by 20,000,000. If this closer union between the empire and the colonies takes place we will be mere likely to see immigrants coming in large numbers from the United States into Canada than to see immigration flowing into the United States from any other country in the world. We should do our share in promoting closer relation with the motherland. We should not halt at the tariff preference which has been granted by the Canadian government to the British people, but back up the efforts of the great Imperial statesman I have mentioned in his efforts for mutual preferential trade relations between the empire and the colonies. Back him up not only by sympathetic words but by acts as well. While this government declined to take up the question of defence on the lines submitted by the imperial authorities, they pledged themselves that they would see to it that our militia would be improved and we should not be deterred by the fear of ex-pense-from fulfilling that pledge. Therefore if the Minister of Militia and Defence gees on with this scheme on the lines suggested, carefully and with a view to the best interests of the militia, I should say that the scheme was a good one. If we are to have a militia force it must to some extent be commensurate with what would be required by the experiences of war. While the enlistment should be smaller than what would be necessary in case of war it is very wise to have all of these auxiliary services, munitions of war, clothing, medical supplies, and camp equipment, in an efficient condition. Not only must we have a full supply of materials but these must be supplemented by proper instruction of those who will have charge of and those who will use them in call of need. All of this will cost a great deal of money. Owing I presume to the large appropriations for which he has had to ask for other purposes, the hon. gentleman has not asked an appropriation for the additional arsenal which he promised us last year or the year before. The hon. gentleman is committed to it but we can wait for it a short time as it is one of the most

important requirements of our system of *defence.

I think I should state, and I forgot to state this, that there is a company now which has approached the government with the view of establishing an arsenal at the city of Ottawa if they can make a contract for the supply of a considerable amount of ammunition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I would not commit myself to the city of Ottawa, but lam glad to hear that it is to be in Ontario. The place it should be located would be a matter, I presume, that the hon. minister and the Major General would be largely responsible for, but it is a matter that requires very careful consideration and therefore I am not prepared to commit myself to any opinion upon it on short notice. I will say, however, that it should be somewhere well west In Ontario. I am very glad to hear that the hon. gentleman is making some progress in that regard. I do not propose to discuss the details of these different votes now because we will be able when we come to consider them in detail to procure any information which the hon. minister has not supplied in his remarks. The most, serious matter of all to be considered is not the establishment of these auxiliaries. I want the hon. gentleman and the government to be seized fully of the responsibility which they are undertaking in asking for these very large sums. That parliament will grant them I have mo doubt. The proposal of the government commits us to these expenditures for years. It is a new departure and it is a scheme which at every step should be most carefully considered because those who follow it will be committed to it, and if there are any mistakes in regard to it the country will be committed to them. This is a comparatively easy thing compared with what I am coming to presently; that Is the providing of the material for the militia, and the question of how it is to be evolved and how the supply is to be main tained. You can establish all these auxiliary services without any trouble. Nearly ail of them will be in the charge of paid men, because those who are in charge of them must be capable of discharging the duties of their positions. The great problem of the militia is in regard to what are called our citizen soldiers. I agree that you cannot make the militia force what it should be and what it is in most countries where it is efficient without establishing these auxiliary services. We have to pay out the money if we are going to have them. But, that is not the difficulty and that is not the hon. gentleman's difficulty now. I call attention to that because I am not satisfied with some features of the hon. gentleman's proposal for reasons which I will give the hon. gentleman presently. I am not saying that I am at all 4204
prepared to oppose this vote or to oppose this proposal. It is my hon. friend who takes the responsibility, but I want him to be seized of the difficulty of the problem which is to raise and keep up even the skeleton, if you call 40,000 men a skeleton, and to get the reserve and keep it. Without this we will simply be wasting the money. We had better accept the doctrine of the timid member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) that we should only provide a police force and put ourselves at the mercy of any country that wishes to step in. I cannot accept that doctrine. I have been brought up in a different school. I believe that what is worth having is worth fighting for. You do not look to see what your chances are if you are a man. You will stand up any way and if you are going to lose your life you will do it in defence of what is worth fighting for. I congratulate the hon. minister on his courage at all events because it requires courage to come down and ask for this large expenditure. It requires still greater courage to admit that this is not for this year only. He has presented it in a way that is proper in such matters as this. I want to call his attention to the fact that this is laying down a wide foundation financially. The people will hold him and his colleagues accountable for it or they will give them credit for it, but the easiest part of the problem is to get the money and to spend it. The difficult problem I am coming to, and it is more than the question of the pay of the militia. Last year the hon. minister promised us a reserve sufficient to make a total of 100,000 men. I will come to that presently. He gave us to-day what I think was a rather optimistic statement of the result of this year's camp and of the state of the militia. The ranks of city regiments have always been and are filled. They have advantages in a way. At the same time you see what the Major General said ; a good deal has to be learned to prepare them for the field. The difficulty with them is the counterpart of what it is with the rural corps. They can drill and assemble together in their drill halls as often as they please, but unless they go away and do some general work they would have a hard time of it if they were turned out suddenly. That can be mended without any great difficulty, but something or other is the matter with the rural militia or else figures and numbers do not speak correctly. My attention was called to this, though I had thought of it before, more strikingly toy the remarks of the hon. member for Haldimand and Monck (Mr. Thompson). Let me say to him that it is very gratifying to find a young member of parliament, with our strong party affiliations, standing up in the way he did and expressing his views as a soldier and as a member of parliament at the same time. He stated what probably some persons might think very unpleasant truths in regard to the militia. I commend him for it and I paid

more attention to what he said on that question under the circumstances than I might otherwise have done. He talks of the state of the camp. I have taken the trouble to prepare some general figures and whatever explanation the hon. Minister of Militia may have made in defence of the Niagara or any other camp I do not think the figures bear him out. The hon. member for Haldi-mand and Monck said :
Am I not justified still further in the assumption that once let the cabinet be convinced that the militia is not even stationary but actually retrogressing this cabin 3t pledged to Britain for improvement, and it must and will gladly meet the situation and destroy the danger?
Well Sir, in all seriousness, after due consideration and recognizing the importance of the assertion, I say here to-day in my place in parliament that the militia, so far as the rural part thereof is concerned, is in infinitely worse plight to-day than it was two years ago, and that in my opinion another year under present conditions will utterly demoralize it.
The reason is not far to seek-it lies in the fifty cent daily wage.
1 do not entirely agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Thompson) that the entire cause is attributable to the pay, tout I do agree with him that the pay is too small. I approve of the suggestion of the minister that the pay should toe graded toy the number of years of service ; tout in view of the condition the force is in at present, I think it would toe wise to increase it at once to 75 cents a day for the first year, and then to scale it up according to the years of service, Like Colonel Thompson, I know the rural militia well. It is true that for some years they have not been turning out as they used to. These men do not want pay in the sense of being hired ; but, all the same, they do not like to toe out of pocket. The first-class men, and that is the kind we want, will not put up with the camp fare, and as they supplement their rations out of their own pockets, they very often f\nd that they are at a loss. It may be said that they should put up with the camp fare, tout you will find tbat men who have the spirit that the minister refers to will not do so. Even members of parliament have looked for an increased indemnity, and so it is through all walks of life ; things have changed since the 50 cents ^ day rate was established. I have the figures here for 1896 and 1897, the last year before the minister came into power and bis first year in office, and the difference is very startling.
The camp in 1896 was under my direction.
