speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Add to that, from the same table, the whole of the city regiments, numbering 11,754, and you have only 23,763 men out of our total force of 40,000. When you could not fill up the small call you made this year, it W'as because there were no more men that you could muster.
The MINISTER OF iMILITIA AND DEFENCE. But my hon. friend will see that we only called out 15,000 and 12,000 responded.

It is my hon. friend who does not see. The fact that you called out only 15,904 shows that you had no more left or you would have filled up the ranks. If you are 25 per cent short of your number, are you going to count all those who are absent as if they were there ? Suppose you want for active service a certain number of men, and you tell the commanding officers of the different regiments to bring out so many men ; they make a call for as many men as they can get until they secure the required number.

Take the case of one company of 40 men. Of these 21 are called out. The captain of that company selects these 21 men. My hon. friend assumes that because all these did not turn out, none of the residue, if they had been asked, would have gone. That is the exception which I take to his argument.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I have been a captain and a colonel, and we do not do any such thing. In that statement Colonel Thompson will bear me out. We say we want so many men, and the word goes out. The necessary number do not turn out. Would we march away without seeing if we could get any others ? Not at all.

Unfortunately, as a rule, the officers of the rural battalions, of one of which I have been a member for a quarter of a century, do not get their men until the morning they are starting for camp ; and it might be that they would not have an opportunity at the last moment of replacing those who failed to turn out.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
There is no use of our discussing this matter. I say that when
you want 21 men out of 45, and you go away with 5 men short, it is conclusive proof that the officers either do not know what they are about or have no other men.
It is conclusive proof that five men who promised to go do not go ; that is all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The trouble with us is always to get enough men. If there were trouble something different might occur, because you could recruit new men. I know' that when the old battalion in Norfolk went to camp, the boys did not start without getting every possible man to make up the required number. The captains were humming around for ten days ; and, as Colonel Thompson complained, and I sympathize with him, ten days is too short a time.
I agree with that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Another thing, which may be due to the shortage the hon. gentleman speaks of, is that very often the battalions go into camp with half the number made up of recruits. It was not so formerly. I remember that for years Colonel Davis, the hon. gentleman's predecessor in command of the 38th and 39th -battalions, used to march to camp with 300 or 400 men, according to whether he had six or eight companies. I say you have only 12,000 men whom you can turn out in the rural districts on an ordinary call for a camp ; and your reserve, whicn was to be 60,000, amounts to only 10,000. Colonel Thompson's figures-and I agree with them-show that the rifle associations would not amount to over 10,000, apart from those belonging to the force. I speak of them from knowledge of several clubs in my own riding. The hon. gentleman spoke moderately and temperately, as he always does, because he did not want to be unduly severe in his criticism.
I say that this is an unsatisfactory and alarming condition, and the minister ought to look into the organization of these rural battalions. I hear things which he may not, but he is responsible and should take timely warning. I tell you, Sir, that the politicians are busy to-day in our militia. When I was in the active militia, the colonels in command-and; I have no doubt the hon. member for Haldimand1 (Mr. Thompson) follows the same course-were always careful to make each corps as non-partisan as possible and to give promotion to every man who deserved it without considering his politics. I was- not a member of parliament then, and we did not care anything about members of parliament. If an officer went courting favours from a member of parliament, he was not allowed to stay very long in the force. There are evidently difficulties of some sort which embarrass our

militia system, there is a lack of inducement to our young men to join the militia, as has been shown by the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Thompson) in the very temperate and measured speech which he made on this subject some time ago, and which could only have been prompted by his sense of duty and his responsibility as commander of a regiment. Whether the trouble lies in the district headquarters or whether it is the politicians who are at the bottom of it, there is an alarming state of affairs, as the hon. member for Haldimand pointed out; and if the Militia Department cannot discover the cause at headquarters, the hon. minister cannot say that he has not been warned by commanding officers and also by one who, although his time of service has passed, still takes a keen interest in the service and is always anxious to promote its efficiency.
In the speech which he made last year the hon. Minister of Militia thus referred to the report of the Major General, for that year, to which I had previously called attention :
Now, I will endeavour, very briefly to refer to some of the matters which the hon. member for South Norfolk has brought before us. In the first place, he has referred to the annual report of the Militia Department, and more particularly to the report of the Major General.
I am sure those who will take the trouble to read that report will agree with him, as I do, that he has not spoken in too high terms of praise of it. While, perhaps, in some of its details, or, possibly, in some of the conclusions of the Major General, I cannot Literally concur, I say that in the main I approve of all that he has said.
I think it is a convenient thing that the Major General, the head of the militia for the time being, should always have a free hand in placing before the people of the country his own views as a professional soldier upon the question of defence, and therefore, during my term of office, and I think it has been, the custom in the past, the Major General of the day has had a free hand to express his real and genuine views in reference to the condition of the militia of the country and in reference to what he thinks ought to be done to improve the condition of the militia.
But what I object to, and have protested against is the refusal of the hou. minister to submit to the House the special report by the general officer commanding to the minister himself. Last year the hon. minister committed himself upon the principle of giving the Major General a ' free hand to express his real and genuine views in reference to the condition, of the militia and in reference to what he thinks ought to be done to improve the condition of the militia ' as I have quoted above, and this year I find in the report of the Major General the following paragraph :
With this report I have the honour also t.o forward another special report to which I have given a great deal of thought, and which contains a broad scheme for the improvement of the militia. If the proposals contained in Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
it are carried out, they will in my opinion conduce to the greater efficiency of the militia.
I have twice before this session requested and insisted upon the minister giving the special report of Lord Dundonald, our new and distinguished Major General to the public.
Let me add that the last time I brought this matter up iu the House my hon. friend the Minister of Militia offered to show that special report to me or to any member of tbe House, but I declined to look at it. The ground I took was that it was not a confidential report, that was not declared to be confidential, and tbe Minister of Militia lias no right at his own sweet will to keep back from the members of this House or the people of this country or those associated with the force whatever propositions the Major General may have submitted. I felt indignant at the refusal to make this report public, and declined to look at what should by right be as public to tbe humblest individual as to any member of parliament. Here is what one of our great independent dailies, the Toronto ' News,' has to say :
Militia reform is fairly active at present in Canada. Yet it seems to move in spasmodic fashion on uncertain lines, and to suffer from lack of prevision and careful planning. For some time the main activity has been in the organization of the highly necessary auxiliary services. Good work has been done. The army service corps scored a brilliant success at Niagara. The bearer companies and field hospitals are excellent troops. The intelligence department has made a good start, and the ordinance corps should prove successful. Much, of course, remains to be done. The engineer arm Is almost altogether neglected, although every day of the South African war showed how indispensable it is. The general officer commanding has no engineer advice at headquarters, and there are no engineers in the permanent force, although an engineer establishment would be of the utmost value to the country for industrial as well as for militia purposes
The provision of auxiliary services falls far short of achieving the organization which the Canadian militia needs.
I commend the hon. minister for having removed some of these deficiencies by the plan he has submitted :
The unreadiness of the fighting services is appalling. For instance, it has been repeatedly pointed out that the proportions of the cavalry, artillery and infantry are absolutely wrong. One lesson of the South African war was the need for heavy guns and pom-poms. Have effective steps been taken to give our artillery these weapons ? The machine gun is indispensable in the field. When Canada sent, an infantry battalion to South Africa, she provided it with two maxims. The second contingent had an automatic gun for each squadron. Yet we have not provided our militia infantry with one machine gun to each battalion. Worse than that-were our battalions to be called out at war strength, it is doubtful whether we could give our men a rifle apiece. We should have an ample supply of ammunition in the country. It is doubtful whether we have more than is needed for target practice.

Many of those defects will be removed by this comprehensive scheme which my hon. friend 1ms brought down, but in this scheme the hon. minister points to something more which the Major General is considering, and what I protest against is that we are called on to vote three and three-quarter million dollars without being informed what the views of the Major General are. The ' News ' proceeds to say :
The list of defects in our force could bo p~o-longed at will. Definiteness and coherence of plan constitute the grand need. We do not wish our militia to find themselves ill-armed-or unarmed-and in hopeless confusion when mobilized. We should go about the work as methodically as we would about the building of a new railway	
It is precisely in this respect that Canada has shown a singular lack of business method. We have an excellent expert. Lord Dundonald is by far the best general officer commanding Canada ever has had. His particular characterise:; is the absence on his part of any desire to professionalize the militia. Ho has not the slightest wish to set up a little army of imitation regulars. He wishes to establish a system for turning out rftal citizen soldiers when the need comes. The great feature of all his suggestions which have been made public is their common sense and the way in which they fit into one another-that is, their coherence.
This expert has prepared a carefully thought-out scheme of organization. We may take it for granted that it is a coherent plan, each part depending on and fitting into the other parts. His propositions have been coolly suppressed. The people of Canada have employed Lord Dundonald and they are not allowed to learn what he recommends. The only excuse put forward is that his report is ' confidential.' That is nonsense. Strategical plans may be kept secret, organization cannot. Lord Dundonald's report, according to the portion which was published, deals with organization, not with strategical plans. It should he placed before the people.
Until we know what our expert has proposed, we are working and spending money in the dark. Piecemeal additions, the raising of new corps here and there, are not sufficient. Coherence of purpose and plan is needed.There is a short way to getting that. Let us know what Lord Duu-donald recommended.
Then :
The ' Canadian Military Gazette,' after remarking that the Canadian soldier needs training, and is anxious to secure it, ' The Gazette ' quotes Lord Dundonald's statement that the ' Canadian soldier takes the greatest interest in anything which his intelligence proves to him is of real practical benefit.' It goes on to say : ' This makes it all the more important that the special report of the General Officer Commanding should not be kept in the pigeon holes of the department at Ottawa. The intelligent Canadian soldier wants to digest it.' ' The Gazette ' speaks in high terms of Lord Dundonald, and observes :	' If the
special reports of experts like Lord Dundonald are to be suppressed, what is the use of placing an expert in the position of General Officer Commanding. We are simply wasting our money and making ourselves the laughing stock of intelligent people.'
This places the matter in a nutshell. We employ an excellent officer, we get him to draw
up a scheme of organization, which, if tried, could not possibly be kept secret, and then we suppress it. For a democratic people we are getting fairly far on the road to autocracy.
Now, I commend these expressions to the minister. I hope be will publish this report. Let us see it; let the people understand it. The bon. gentleman is lessening bis own usefulness as-head of the force, as well as hurting the feelings of officers and men of the militia, by not letting them know what this report contains. Nor is it just to the general. It is not respectful to the intelligent people of this country that such a state of tilings should exist. If the report were confidential in anyway or could be considered so, the general would certainly have so stated.

My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) says that the report to which he refers says it was not confidential. It may not have been marked ' confidential ' but I think I am the best judge whether it was confidential or not. The report was a scheme of defence, and was not, in my judgment, such a report as should be published to the world. When I referred to a former report it was to that of General O'Grady Haly, but the very nature of my observations shows that I referred to the ordinary report of the year reviewing the work of the militia of the year. We have done the same tiling with Lord Dundonald In this case. He had a free hand. He said what he wanted to say. Not a word has been changed, not a ' t ' crossed or an ' i ' dotted in change of liis report. But, besides this, he made a special report, involving a very large expenditure. That report came into my band twenty-four hours before the whole report had to go to the printer. I had not read it or submitted it to my colleagues, and it would have been out of the question that such a report as that should have been sent to the printer to be published to the world before the minister should have an opportunity of considering it. I have kept that report in my own hands. I have used it and am using it. It was an official report for the advantage of the government of the country. There are parts of it that will be published; I shall have great pleasure in publishing them. But so far as that report involves a heavy expenditure which the government had not decided to make I felt it would he highly improper to publish it. that it is a thing that would not be done in England or anywhere else.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: What did the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) say was the nature of this report ?

I said it was practically a scheme of defence. We had a committee sitting here in 1898. for which we paid a very considerable sum of money, which made a

report which has never seen the light of day. It was printed by the Defence Committee under the imperial government. It is something secret. Lord Dundonald's report was of a similar character, and one that at any rate for the time being should he treated as confidential.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Lord Dundonald said it was a broad scheme for the improvement of the militia. If it is this as well as the other, why not publish the part of it that can be published ?
I have said that that would be done, and I have given part of it to-day.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman used it in his own speech. But that is not very satisfactory to hon. gentlemen on this side who have had no opportunity to read this report. How can we discuss it when we have had no opportunity to read it ?
No one on this side has had it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Except the hon. minister himself.

Who ever heard of a minister not having the advantage, and, if he saw fit, the exclusive advantage at the outset, of the advice of his principal technical officer ? Who ever heard of the government not having that advantage ? And who ever heard of such an officer's report being published to the world before the government had had an opportunity of deciding whether they would adopt the suggestion set forth in it or not ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I was pointing out the effect of this course. The Major General, who is the chief officer of the Militia Department, makes a certain report to the department. That report is treated as a strictly private matter. The minister may differ very materially from the Major General with respect to the contents of that report. But I think parliament should be in a position to say which, in our judgment, is right.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) thinks it is in accordance with the principles and practice of responsible government that an official of the Militia Department should have the right to put forward his views to the people before the minister has made up his mind whether he will adopt those views or not ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I will go so far as to say that there is no usfc having an expert military man come to this country for the purpose of suggesting what would be in the interests of the militia if his recommendations are not carried out.
I take the responsibility.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) a question if he will allow me. I did not quite understand his remarks regarding politics entering the militia. Did I understand him to say that this was one cause why the force was not in as good a condition as it might be V

No. I said I thought it worth the minister's while to be careful, to make inquiries lest such a thing might exist; and that if it did exist it might explain some matters that we could not explain otherwise. Now, I would say just one word in reply to the minister. According to my idea the hon. gentleman was not' quite correct in his reference to the Major General. The Major General is not an officer of the department; he is commander pf the militia. The minister is responsible for his actions, and above him, but
I think he is an officer of the Canadian government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: He is. But the hon. minister said he was an officer of the department
Well, he is. He is certainly not controller of the department, not the 'boss' of the department-not now, at any rate.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The hon. minister told us to-day of his arrangement about the stores department. I said I commended the hon. gentleman for his arrangement for the ordnance stores department. But if the position of the Major General in regard to it is to be circumscribed, friction will arise, and the arrangement will be of little good. I laid it down before and I do it now that the general is under the minister. The minister is under our system responsible. His position is political.
That is right.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: And the minister cannot divest himself of that responsibility.
That is right.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
When we use the word political,' we use it in the sense in whicli the hon. member for Haldimand and* Monck uses it. But this matter is different.
I cannot be satisfied without an assurance from the hon. minister that the Major General would ever have put in his general report what he did about the special report unless he were perfectly willing that the hon. minister should show it anywhere, because, judging from what I have heard of him from all quarters, he is the last man who would do anything else. I believe the Major General put that in there not to decide whether it was to be used or not, but to 1 let it be known that he did so. There was

one thing that I forgot to mention in my remarks, and that was the singular absence from his report of any mention of the scheme in regard to the reserve, &c., outlined by the hon. minister. That is the reason X read that little clause where he made the single remark about putting every regimental establishment on a war footing and stating that within each unit there would be the germ of a reserve. I knew that the Major General had written something else about that, and it must have been in the report originally, because I saw a Major General's report so barren of reference to the strength of the different establishments and no mention at all of a reserve except in, this one little paragraph, notwithstanding that this was the most fruitful of all subjects upon which he could have written. Of course, it is not for him to dictate to the hon. minis-! ter, nor will he attempt to do so. However, the hon. minister takes the responsibility, and if he sees fit, he has the might to do so, but in my opinion it is not a case where 1 might will make right ', but 'I think it is a great mistake if the Major General is to be made an automaton. If he has anything to suggest to the minister, let us know what he says when it comes to the regulation of the militia. We want a man, and we have got him for a Major General, and it is a grave step for the minister to repress his special report to which he says he has 'given a great deal of thought and which, contains a broad scheme for the improvement of the militia. If the proposals contained in it are carried out they will in my opinion conduce to the greater efficiency of the militia.'

I think my hon. friend will agree with me that the proper means of communication with this House and with the country from the Major General is through the mouth of the minister, particularly when there is a question of policy involved.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Certainly, it must be through the minister's mouth.

Mr. Chairman, while I am ready and willing to admit that there are many admirable features of this scheme which have been outlined by the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence to the committee, I must confess also that I feel great disappointment, as I am sure every other member of the militia force-at least, that portion of the militia force which is included in the infantry-will feel that the matter has not been dealt with that bravery that we would naturally expect from the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence. I refer to increased pay for the men. We bear a great deal from the hon. minister's side of the House about the growing times. We hear of every department of the public service benefiting by these growing times. Almost every -branch of the militia service, according to the hon. minister's own statement, is feeling the benefit of these growing times, and yet what are the boue and sinew of the defence of this country to get from the great expenditure of money that these hon. gentlemen are indulging in?-not one dollar, not one cent. I propose, as far as I can, in my humble way, to bring to the attention of the hon. minister some matters which I venture to hope may at least change his opinions a little, though they may not change his actions. I would first refer to some of the comparisons which the hon. minister has made in his speech to the committee, and which, I think, are not exactly fair. In the first place, reference has been made by the hon. minister to the percentages of the attendance at the district camps, by way of comparison, in the years 1900 and 1903. I am sure the hon. minister must have forgotten that in 1900 the full strength of the different regiments was called into camp.

That is just why I made the comparison. I said, to show that the system adopted this year has not been such a terrible failure, I will take a year when the full force was called out, and I will prove that the percentage of attendance this year of those called out is as good, if not better, than the percentage of the whole force when it was called out. That was the point.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I think the hon. minister's point is not well taken, because the percentage in 1900 was of the whole force of the militia which was called into camp, while the percentage taken for this present year is only based on the estimate that twenty-one men belonging to the different companies were called into camp. Therefore, the percentage, based on the whole force, would not have the same effect, it seems to me, as the percentage based on balf the strength.
Oh, yes; just thd same.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I will try and convince the hon. minister that it is not so.

The percentage in 1900 was calculated by me as the percentage of those who attended relatively to the total number of the militia called out. The percentage this year was the ratio of the number who attended to the number called out.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Certainly, that is exactly what I say. If it was so difficult in this present year to get even the same percentage of half the strength, surely there must be something wrong. It was not so difficult in 1900 and in the years preceding that to get the same percentage of the full strength as it is now we get the same percentage^ of half the strength. There must be something wrong if we cannot induce men to go to

camp to make 25 per cent or 50 per cent of tlie strength with the number called out this year, which was only 21 men to a company. In regard to that, I simply want to give the hon. minister a little of the experience I have had in my own regiment. But, before I go into that, I wish to point out to the hon. minister how unfair I believe the comparison to be which he made. We will take, for instance, military districts Nos. 3 and 4, which assembled at Kingston. It is very well known that about one-third of the number of men at Kingston consisted of cavalrymen, and I think it is well known that nearly every troop or squadron of cavalry was full strength at Kingston. In instituting that comparison he should have left out the cavalry and taken into account the infantry alone. It is not a fair comparison when you take troops, each squadron of which had its full strength, and add that to .the number of those who had suffered by reason of want of pay. In regard to cavalry, I wish to state that in my own county we have had a great deal of trouble in keeping up the full strength which is called for, that is, one-quarter of the strength of the regiment.
It is well known to every militiaman that the cavalry and artillery are more favourably treated by the Militia and Defence Department than the infantry. Take for instance the cavalry squadrons that were recruited in my own county. I know as a matter of fact that the officers of that cavalry regiment went through two townships in my county and secured all the horses they wanted for fifty cents per day. These horses were secured for the men of the cavalry squadrons who were not owners of horses and very few of the members were in this position. The consequence of this was that the men of that cavalry regiment almost to a man received a dollar a day and the horses were paid for at the rate of fifty cents per day. That is what I have to contend with in my county and there is no doubt that where men can secure one dollar a day by going into the cavalry they will always prefer it to serving in the infantry for 50 cents. I wish to point out to the minister what appears to me and to many others an absurdity, that one dollar a day should be allowed for a horse and only fifty cents for a man. The hon. minister has stated that he knows of men paying out one dollar and one dollar and a half a day for horses. That may be perfectly time in cities where wealthy gentlemen join tlie mounted infantry and will pav any price for a horse which will make a good appearance. I can assure the hon. minister that in the country-and I do not think my county an exception-any number of horses can be procured at fifty cents a day. It seems to me that the cavalry and artillery are placed on a higher basis altogether than the infantry and it is therefore impossible Mr. WARD.
to secure men to fill up the different companies of infantry even if these companies are called upon to take only one-third of their strength into camp. I had almost persuaded two young men in the county to iake two lieutenancies in my regment, but finally they refused altogether to go into the regiment simply because it was utterly impossible to get the men at fifty cents a day and they said it was a perfect farce for them to attempt to pose as officers when they could not have the men. I mention these facts only in order that the minister may take them into consideration. It may be too late to do anything this year but next year when we may have a Bill making some changes in the rate of pay of the militia the minister might consider this matter favourably. I can only say that the proposition of the minister to add five cents per year of service to the daily pay of the men who have served more than one year would be utterly inadequate.
I did not mention the sum ; I-certainly would not think of five cents being sufficient.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I think the minister has stated that on previous occasions.
Nothing less than ten cents I think. ,
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Even with ten cents it would require three years to entitle a man to the pay of eighty cents per day. I can only say from my own experience in the county which I have the honour to represent and in which I command a regiment, that unless something is done this, as the hon. member for Haldimaud (Mr. Thompson) has said, is only the beginning of the disintegration of the rural corps.

I have listened with much interest to the debate that has taken place and to the statement of the Minister of Militia and Defence which contains many propositions that I think will meet with the hearty approval of the country at large. I believe that a careful investigation into the conditions of the rural corps will demonstrate that there is a manifest decadence in the military ardour of the young men of this country compared with that of fifteen, twenty or twenty-five years ago. There must be some cause for this. In the county where I live the officers of the various companies find it difficult to get a contingent of men to go to camp for the annual drill although in former years they had no difficulty. One of the causes, I presume, is the very insufficient pay given to the men. Fifty cents per day is so ridiculously small that it does not come up to what might be called an indemnity. Had it not been that the county council of the county in which I live have added to that rate of pay twenty-

five cents per man, year after year, the corps would not be in as good condition as it now is. I have been a member of the county council for years and every time that question came up there was opposition to it on the ground that the municipal council having no authority or control over the volunteers, it was the duty of the federal government to pay the men, although it was generally admitted that the present rate is very far from being sufficient. There may be other causes. When the young men see the condition in which the drill halls erected twenty-five or thirty years ago are to-day, wrecks and ruins in all parts of the country, they must be impressed with the thought that the government have but little interest in the rural corps. They see that while large sums are spent in cities for building large and expensive armouries, the drill halls throughout tlie: country are allowed to go to ruin. In the town where I live there is a large drill hall, and in connection with it a well fitted armoury in which arms and clothing could be well stored were it not for the fact that the roof is bad. The officers of the district have made appeals again and again for sufficient money to make the roof tight but without success so that the armoury is practically useless for purposes of storage.
The proposal of the minister that the pay of the men should be graded in proportion to the number of annual drills they have put in will meet with the hearty approval of the House and of the country at large. It is a fact that on many occasions when the officers of a company desire to make up a contingent they have to pick up a few loose men who happen to be out of employment. These men of course enlist for three years, but, when the next camp comes around they may not be in the country. That they should be paid at the same rate as men who have put in two, three, five or even ten annual drills is absurd and ridiculous. As it is now they receive the same rate as men who have learned their drill and who have had sufficient interest in military matters to go to camp year after year. An increase of ten or even twenty cents a day would be inadequate, and I think that; this matter should be met in a fairly generous and liberal spirit. There is sufficient military spirit in this country to justify the additional expense that would be involved in paying a fair rate for the few days annual drill so as to give the men a reasonable indemnity and tend to arouse to some extent the military ardour of the young men of Canada. I think that something might perhaps be done with regard to the encouragement of rifle ranges throughout the country. The city corps have the advantage over the rural corps in this respect. It will be admitted by the minister also, that the armament of the rural corps cannot very well be dispensed with. You can get good companies in the city and have them turn out well, because they have better advantages for assembling and for constant drill. But yet, in the rural corps you have men who in wars such as the recent war in South Africa have already learned the art, or who from boyhood up, have handled a rifle and are naturally good shots. The members of the rural corps have also that resource which perhaps men accustomed to city life have not; they possess that initiative which is so necessary in military work at the present day. Therefore, in view of the decadence in the ardour and military spirit which characterized the rural corps in the past, I appeal to the minister that there should be a careful inquiry made into its causes.

On the 30th of June last I made some rather extended remarks upon the Canadian militia, and on looking up that speech I find I prefaced it by saying :
At this late date in the session I will not speak at any great length.
Hear, hear.

If I had that feeling at that time, you can readily understand that since July, August and September have taken to themselves wings, and now that October is speedily following in their wake, I shall not ask this committee to listen to me at any length at all, and especially so in view of the very excellent and extended addresses of the Minister of Militia and of the gentlemen who spoke after him. I shall not attempt to touch in detail the many points which the minister raised, but I shall rather confine myself for five or ten minutes to a discussion of that, to my mind very important point, an increase of pay for the rural militia. I have the most excellent feeling of friendliness for the Minister of Militia, and I believe I am not altogether lacking in discipline in the party as in the army.
Hear, hear.

I will say, however, that I have not got up to apologize for what I said with regard to the rural militia, nor yet to recant because I did not study that question so much from the books as I did from the actual camps themselves. I have been there ; I have seen. Referring, in order, to what the minister said : First of all, as to this large expenditure of $1,300,000. I believe that this is an excellent thing, and, with the member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale), I join in congratulating the minister upon his courage in making the announcement of this vote, not apologetically, as we are so accustomed to do when dealing with militia matters in this country, but bravely and boldly, as if he had something to be proud of-as I think he had in making that statement. I compliment the minister that he was further courageous enough to

go on and say that this rote would not be for one year only, but might even be for five years in succession. The minister has told us to-day, what many of us knew before ; he told us that we have in Canada something less than 40,000 arms of modern make-referring, of course, to the rifles. We all know that supply would ibe inadequate in case of serious trouble. We know that our militia is formed on the skeleton basis -that is a word that I did not coin myself ; it is a well-known word in the militia-and that in case of war we would expect to increase our companies from a strength of 42 to 125 in all. What would be the use of increasing these companies to 125 men if you only had 42 rifles for the 125 men ? The other fellows could not light very well with pitchforks and clubs, and therefore you must furnish each of these men with a rifle. I therefore say that the minister is doing no more than his duty, and this government is doing no more than its duty, in voting even a considerable sum, such as this, towards furnishing this increased armament, which will put one rifle in the hands of one man for whatever force we may find it necessary to put iu the field in case of trouble. The same thing applies to the armament of the artillery, with which, however, I am not quite so conversant. I believe, Sir, that every cent of this expenditure will be justified ; that not one cent of it will be found fault with by the intelligent electors of Canada. It does seem to me rather a pity, however, that when we are expending this comparatively large sum. we cannot add just a little more to it. It would not look very much added on to' the end of that $1,300,000 -or to the end of $3,750,000, which I understood the member for South Norfolk to say will be the total expenditure of the Militia Department for all purposes this year-
Including public works.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Including, of course, the drill sheds, which really are a militia expenditure as much as anything else. I gave figures to prove, and I believe that these figures are unquestioned, that by paying one dollar per day instead of fifty cents per day to all the militia men of Canada, it would only cost something like $225,000 additional ; and that if the increase of pay applied only to the rural militia, it would cost about half that amount.
I gave reasons why there might fairly be a difference made between the rural and city corps in regard to pay. I would not weary the House by repeating my argument at length on that point, but one of the main reasons which might commend itself to the common sense of every hon. gentleman here is that city soldiers all perform their drill at night, when their day's wage has been earned, whereas the country soldier leaves his home for twelve whole days in the year. The question of pay is much Mr. THOMPSON (Haldimand).
more important to the rural soldier than to the city soldier. More than that, one point which I made, and which cannot be satisfactorily answered, is this : The city soldier is not troubled about the question of pay, the best evidence of which is that he does not draw his pay. If you had your city regiments but half filled up, and if the men that did go into these regiments drew their pay, it might be fair to argue that the low pay was responsible for the depletion of the ranks of the city corps. But when you find these city corps full to overflowing, and the men in the ranks not even drawing their pay, but turning it into a central fund for the purpose of a holiday on Thanksgiving Day, or the 24th of May, or the 1st of July ; then I say that the pay is not at all a question with the city men. My object is not to fill anybody's pocket, but to fill the regiments of this country with men, as they should be filled ; and, therefore, if the city regiments are already filled by the pay they have got, I have enough respect for these city regiments, enoygh confidence in their loyalty to the militia; to hold the theory that they would be the first to say : If our country brethren must have half a dollar more than we, in order to have good country regiments, give them the half dollar a day, it does not affect us at all. I do not believe in there being any jealousy between the city corps and the country corps ; I do believe in the esprit de corps of the whole force, and I have reason for my belief in a long personal experience. Now, Sir, there is more than one thing to consider in regard to the camps of instruction, when you come to the question of the men who attend them. It is always a dangerous thing simply to count noses ; you have to look to the quality of the men, and I want to say that from the experience I had iin two "camps this year-and I think my brother officers will bear me out-not only were the regiments much under strength, but the physique of the men who did go into camp was so inferior that in actual active service, a very large percentage of these men would never be able to make a campaign. .1 do not believe that in this commercial country of Canada you can get a $1.50 man for 50 cents. It is all very well to talk about loyalty and patriotism calling the men into the ranks. Canada has just as much patriotism as any other country. Let a war, or a serious danger, menace this country, and you will find the fellows flocking to the colours. But we are talking now of a peace footing ; a preparation in time of peace for a possible state of war, and I say that it is nothing against a man's patriotism that he does not want to go into camp for 50 cents a day when he earns $1.50 by remaining at home.
I would like to ask : How many members of this hon. House hold His Majesty's commission ? Not 3 per cent. And would any gentleman say that the members of this House, who are not members of the militia,

are disloyal because they are not in the ranks ? Not at all. Being in the ranks of the active militia is no proof of loyalty, disloyalty, patriotism or the reverse.
But we are living in a commercial age.
1 understood the minister himself to say that he believed in indemnifying the soldiers. He did not believe that a young Canadian who went to camp should want to make money, but he believed he should be indemnified. As I understand the word * indemnify,' it means to save from loss. How can a man who earns $1.50 a day be indemnified on 50 cents a day ? He is just a dollar short. Therefore I say that the present pay does not indemnify the men at all. I do not believe that we require to raise the pay of soldiers to an equality with that of men in commercial life ; but we have to approximate it. Give the boys a dollar a day, and the ranks will be filled, and not with the class of men we have at present, a considerable proportion of whom are unfit, but with the best young men that can be got in our country. The Major General Commanding has recommended, the minister has adopted the recommendation, and it has been decided, not to call out the full strength of our force each year, but only about one-half of it. One hundred thousand men, I believe, are to be the total militia force. Of these 60,000 are not to be called out at all, but are to be enrolled as a reserve subject to call in time of war ; and each man is to be given a rifle and trained in rifle shooting. Of the other 40,000 the minister proposes to call out all the city corps and about half the country corps. The remaining half of the country corps are I fear in limbo. They are betwixt and between. If only one-half are to be called out, what a, bagatelle it would be to give them $1 a day. It would only amount to one-half the figures I have already given to the House. It would cut down the cost to 14 cents per head of the population of Canada. I estimated that it would cost four cents per head to give $1 a day to the whole force, or two and one-half cents per head to give $1 a day to the whole rural force. If you only call out half the rural force, one and one-fourth cents for every man woman and child in Canada, would give the men a fair wage, and would fill our regiments to overflowing with the best bone and sinew of the country. It is not much to ask. I know that the minister has it not in his power to increase the pay of the militia. That is regulated by the Militia Act. But we in this House have power to amend that Act, and I believe that next session a new Act is to be introduced. If so, one thing we should see to is that power is given to the minister of the day to regulate the pay of the soldiers, so that it will bear some proportion to the current rate of wages in commercial life. I am rather sorry that the whole force is not going to be called out every year. Iam afraid speaking from experience, that such a turnout as is here indicated will not encourage that spirit in the officers which will bring good men into the officers' mess. The average captain does not want to have simply three or four men trailing behind him. He wants to have a fair company, and the colonel wants to have a regiment to command which is somewhat larger than a large company. You have to consider the effect this system will have on the men. The minister has very properly said that the militia officers must be educated men. That is true ; but you have first to have your militia officer before you can begin this process of education ; and unless you give the officer something to be proud of in his unit, you are not going to get him to join the force. I believe that is what this is coming to. Therefore, I regret that the whole force is not to be called out. But time will tell. There are those who say we can get along well enough on the present pay. I do not think so. I believe that if you took a poll of the present militia force, you would find 99 per cent of the officers in favour of paying at least 75 cents a day, and nearly as many preferring $1 per day. It is all very well to talk of grading the pay ; but even then you must give the men enough to get them in the first year before you can have them in the second or the third year. This is to be a kind of corps d'elite ; as the minister says, they are to be selected men. If we are to get rid of a certain percentage of men who are not by any means selected, and to get these selected men on the roll, I really think it will be necessary to pay $1 a day. If you just want ordinary men, 75 cents a day might do. But if you are going to get the class of men we should have, when you are cutting the number down one-half, they should be paid at least $1 a day. Now, I believe I have already transgressed the time limit. I understand, that the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes), whose speeches are always instructive, is to follow. I believe I misled him in saying that I was going to speak only a short time, and therefore I tender him my sincere apology.

I do not on this occasion intend to make any extended remarks. There were a number of questions which I desired during the session to bring before the minister and the Hpuse ; but with that usual fatality which characterizes such intentions, the remarks are put off to the end of the session, and the session closes, and there is nothing done. However, I have taken the liberty and the opportunity of conversing with the minister from time to time, and, although we are politically opposed, and he is a great warrior, none of us on this side of the House are afraid to approach him to lay suggestions before him for the benefit of the militia ; and I am glad to say that he is always

ready to receive those suggestions in the kindest manner. I will just run over a tew points which I propose discussing.
I want to supplement what my bon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Thompson) stated; about the importance of having an esprit de corps in any camp. The various corps this year marched out from their quarters to the brigade camps, and there was scarcely a regiment headed by its band. The scattered few collected from each company fell in at the battalion headquarters, and took the back streets to the station, carrying their knapsacks and rifles, and got into the train as quietly as possible ; and they came back in the same way. That is not the way a regiment should go into camp.
Another thing I wish to speak of are the pensions to those who were seriously injured in the South African war. I hare already had the honour of bringing this subject twice before the minister this session, and he promised to give it his consideration. There are many young men. It is not necessary for me to speak at length on this question, as we have had it up twice before this session. There are many young men in Canada whose claims should be considered in this connection, notably one who had both eyes shot out, and others with both arms shot off, another with his leg shot off. These young men, by reason of their wounds, have lost their positions, and have practically to depend on their pensions. I am satisfied that the country will endorse the Minister of Militia if he takes the same bold stand on this matter that he has taken on other matters, and insists on the Minister of Finance giving him a grant to supplement for all time to come the pensions which the British government is paying to these men. I am sure the hon. gentleman need not. fear the hon. member for I.abelle (Mr. Bourassa) in doing so, for the hon. gentleman's bark, as every one knows, is worse than his bite'. I purposed discussing at considerable length the permanent corps and the basis on which it is established.
I withdrew a notice of motion which I had on the order paper regarding rifle practice in the schools of this Dominion, but nevertheless my opinion is that every boy of the age of eighteen should be trained in the use of the rifle. If Canada had her young men trained to-day in miniature rifle practice, not the long range-because as I have again and again pointed out those of us who learned shooting in the old days learned it, not with the long range rifle but with the old muzzle loading Lee-Enfield with a snap-cap-we would in ten years be invincible. There is a most excellent device in the department whereby one can test the accuracy of his aim. If these machines could be obtained cheaply enough, they would be capital things to have at the headquarters of every company in order that the boys might learn rifle shooting. If our youth were trained in this

practice, the entire forees of the United States could not make an invasion of Canada which would be effective for twenty-four hours.
I purposed also discussing the position of the permanent officers of the force, such as the district officers commanding, and the district staff adjutants, and the functions they should perform. They are very excellent officers indeed, but in order to carry out to the letter the plan of the minister and the idea he has in forming his brigades and divisions, it is absolutely necessary that retired officers who have passed the age limit and have served five years in command of regiments-and who are the men who, in time of trouble, will command the army corps-should be given an opportunity of gaining experience in that service. The question of the pay of the officers and men I also purposed discussing at length.
I notice in the estimates that the hon. minister proposes to have monuments erected on some battle fields, including the battle field of Fort Erie. I commend this expenditure and would suggest that he should lose no time in placing these monuments on every battle field. We should have monuments at Chateauguay and Chrysler's Farm, and various other historic grounds. I do not know that Queenston Heights has any monument except that erected to General Brock. But that was not erected by the Canadian government. There is nothing better calculated to inspire in the youth of our country loyalty and love for their native land than these records of great deeds of valour. I have no doubt that the monument at the city hall in this city, commemorating the men who fell in South Africa stirs in the hearts of our rising population the throb of patriotism-the noblest sentiment that can actuate men.
I also purposed saying a few words in connection with the Ross rifle, and I did purpose drawing attention to some remarks contained in the report of the intercolonial conference on that subject. Although I am a Britisher and have endeavoured to prove myself so to the core, still I do not believe that the British war office should dictate to the people of the Dominion what rifle they should use. I believe that our people are perfectly qualified to select for themselves. The hon. minister has rightly taken the precaution that the bore of the rifle which we use shall be the same as that of the imperial rifle, and that the ammunition for the Boss rifle shall be the same as that used in the imperial army.
I want to say this

and I have had the opportunity to obtain as good knowledge of rifles as most men of the community-that in so far as the action of the Ross rifle is concerned, I consider it much ahead of any other rifle yet manufactured. I had the privilege of meeting the inventor of this action just after the South African war, and in discussing the defects of the present

British rifle, I pointed out what I .considered three serious defects. He asked me if I would be good enough to go and see the arm he invented. I did so and he showed me the Ross rifle of which I had hitherto heard nothing, and in that rifle each of the three defects that I pointed out have been removed. I therefore have no hesitation in endorsing the Ross rifle,
I also purposed saying a few words with reference to the military college and intended touching on the water suppply. I have learned, however, since that a new system of purifying the water supply is about to be introduced there, a similar plan to that adopted in Winnipeg. The Winnipeg water comes from Bake Manitoba underground! and goes through a purifying process which rids it of alkali.
It is the Philadelphia system which is adopted in the college.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
That is on the same principle, but the system used in the college would not suit at all. However, the hon. minister will no doubt succeed in getting pure water. I am satisfied that the best way would be to have a pump station on Garden Island and force the water over to the college.
I purposed discussing the advisability of having inland arsenals to be placed as far inland as convenient from the frontier, so that in case of war we would not be liable to have them cut off. We ought to have two or three establishments for the manufacture of ammunition, owing to the peculiar nature of our country and also owing to the fact that the new transcontinental road is not yet constructed. That would give a supply of ammunition to the great centres of the Dominion in case of trouble. Talk of your pom-poms and big guns, but after all it is the rifle and the Maxim guns that unman the enemy and empty the saddles.
I commend also the item in relation to the military survey and the establishment of the intelligence branch. I congratulate the hon. minister and the major general commanding on having secured an able officer, Colonel Dennison, to take command of that department. He has proved himself a most efficient officer, wherever he has been, especially in South Africa. The only fault I would find is with the smallness of the sum which the hon. minister is asking. In keeping up a militia system, we must always recognize that our neighbours to the south are an aggressive race, just as we are, and we must always bear in mind . that the possibility may arise some time of war between Canada and the United States. I have a paper in my desk of a fire-eating nature, but not very dangerous, which was sent me from the wild and woolly west. This paper is published in Kansas. It suggests that the American government should
settle this Alaska boundary business by simply gobbling up Canada.
They would have a hot time doing it.

Undoubtedly, the Nova Scotia and Ontario boys would give a gcod account of themselves. The point I wish to make is this-that every foot of land upon the border between Canada and the United States, as well as the country for a considerable distance this side of the border, should be surveyed, and maps should! be made so as to be at the disposal of officers and men in case of war. I have before me the report of the military commission in Great Britain. Every one knows that at the beginning of the South African war Great Britain had no maps even of her own Cape Colony and Natal. We had to go through by pure guesswork. It was my privilege to be intelligence officer to two columns in that war. I never found a map that was of service. It was far better to take the data furnished by people who had travelled over the country, and of Kaffirs and others who lived in various localities. After a time we were able to get hold of a number of the Boer maps of the Transvaal, Orange Free State, and other parts. These were all scaled and made up with the greatest nicety. I commend the step that the minister proposes. But the amount will need to be greatly increased year by year in order that the country may be surveyed and these maps prepared.
I do not apologize to the House or to the country for saying that we should be ready to meet the United) Staets. I believe in being friendly with our friends to the south. I have always been friendly with them and respected them. But there is no use in shutting our eyes to the fact that there is an element there, as there is in every country, that is antagonistic to their neighbours. That element _very nearly asserted itself under President Cleveland. In carrying out the laws of this country, laws recognized by the government of the United States, a thieving Yankee ship was captured in British waters while engaged in taking fish that rightly belonged to our own fishermen. President Cleveland called upon the governors of the several states along the border to know how many men they could throw upon the Canadian border inside of a week.
Was that despatch published ?

It was a private message. Nobody knew anything about it. it was entirely secret. They went from governor to governor of these states, and it was found that they could not put 50,000 men on the Canadian border inside of two weeks. Otherwise the chance is fifty to one that trouble would have been sprung upon us at that time without notice. We

might as well let it be known frankly, as Palmerston did on one occasion, that we have rights and are prepared to defend them. We have boys who know how to nse firearms, and I trust that in a short time we shall have officers in great numbers trained to take command of these lads. And, if once that status is arrived at, any enemy, I care not who, will hesitate long before they will set foot across the Canadian border.
I purposed also taking up a very delicate subject, a rule that has been promulgated that, for the future, no lieutenant in the permanent force shall marry without the permission of the bead of the department. I would suggest that a better way of meeting this question would be for the Minister of Militia and Defence to increase the pay of these permanent corps officers, so that every one of them can support the little girl of his choice in, at all events, a fair degree of comfort. And as soon as any of these boys finds the young lady who, he thinks, would be fit to become his partner in life, he should be encouraged to take such a partner rather than debarred from doing so.
Another point that I purposed touching upon -at some length, if opportunity had offered, was the question of medals to the first men of the fourth contingent who went to South Africa. X would just point out to the minister that these men had reached Cape Town harbour. They went to South Africa in full expectation of engaging actively in the war. Disaster had fallen on British arms and the hearts of all these men beat high in the hope of being able to serve their country in the field. They reached Table Bay; they were within the three-mile limit and would have landed had not orders been received sending them around to Durban. I maintain that the minister would be justified in insisting on the British government recognizing the claims of these men. It was while they were proceeding under orders to Durban peace was declared. If the rule is enforced as now proposed, these men will be deprived of the only recognition, the only remuneration, that many of them coveted for their services in South Africa.
I also pui-posed taking up the question of the permanent corps, as contrasted with the rural corps, and the rural corps as contrasted with the city corps. But time will not permit me to do so on this occasion, and so I shall defer it until another time.
The question of pay is an important one. As the hon. minister knows, this matter was brought up by me early in the session. I suggested that, in all fairness to the men, the pay should be increased and graded. I believe that 50 cents per day should be tbe pay for the first year and increased by 25 cents for the subsequent years. Suppose that that had been brought into force, in the coming year a man would receive 75 cents per day. In the third year be would

receive St per day, with a corresponding increase for non-commissioned ranks. I do not think the country would mind the expenditure much, and I think the minister would do well to look at that aspect of the case. However, I will take that up at greater length on another occasion. For many years I have objected to a horse being paid SI per day in camp and a man being paid only 50 cents per day in camp. If the minister is going to graduate the pay of a man, let him graduate the pay of a horse. Pay the horse that comes into camp for training 50 cents per day. The horse that comes in for a second year for training and is partly familiar with the bridle and knee-action, let it be paid 75 cents per day ; and the third year it will be worth $1 per day. In other words, let the man and the horse be graduated year by year. I am satisfied that it would not cost the country such a very great sum, and the force would be much benefited. On this question of pay, I desire to refer to the excellent speech of the hon. member for Flaldimand (Mr. Thompson). I had not the pleasure of hearing that speech, but I have taken occasion to read it. That hon. gentleman says that the falling off in the percentage of attendance in the various camps is due entirely to the fact that the pay is so small. I have endeavoured to point out, as occasion offered, how the falling off in attendance was brought about, what the cause of the lack of energy is on the part of the officers, and why it is that the military spirit which was characteristic of this whole country and is still characteristic of parts of it has waned. It is due to the fact that we have no efficient system for training officers. As tbe minister knows. I gave my views on this question again and again to the House. And, if I have an opportunity. I will again point out to the House that if a proper plan be pursued in the training of officers it will have the effect of infusing a military spirit into the country. I do not believe in a great increase in the permanent force. Why should two hundred men be placed in the city of Montreal ? In the whole city of Chicago-and it is one of the toughest cities on earth-the United States government does not keep anything like that number. There are a number at Fort Sheridan, but that is twenty or thirty miles away, and they are kept there because it is a good place to drill. From a police standpoint they' are entirely unnecessary in the Dominion of Canada. If we want police along the water stretches of the frontier, at the canals and at the Soo let us employ them as a permanent police, let us not enroll them as soldiers and then have them called out to preserve law and order. I have too high a respect for the people of Canada to think that it is necessary, in order to preserve order, to have men stationed over them with fixed bayonets. I believe in making the permanent corps an educational rather than

a military institution. I would have our officers appointed to positions on the basis of knowledge rather than of military rank. I would have the men attending these classes graded according to their military education so that those of similar knowledge would be placed in the same squads and conducted from class to class until they would arrive at such a stage of instruction as would be desired. In regard to pay we all have read the famous lines of Bobby Burns which conclude with this stanza :
Glory is the soldier's price The soldier's wealth is honour.
I am satisfied from the statements which have fallen from the lips of the hon. member for Haldimand and Monck (Mr. Thompson) when he pointed out that the city corps throughout Canada are kept to full strength and never draw one cent of pay
They are not kept at any-think like full strength.
If they are not kept up at anything like full strength in a one horse town like St. Thomas it is because their officers and non-commissioned officers are not up to what they ought to be.
I would like to stick up for the one horse town of St. Thomas ; it is equal to Lindsay at any rate. While the strength is kept up in St. Thomas there are other towns where it is not.
Wherever j'ou find a rural or city corps that is not kept up you will find a deficiency in the spirit of the officers and non-commissioned officers.
Would that apply to Haldimand ?
Certainly, if the officers and non-commissioned officers in Col. Thompson's regiment were all living up to their duty, that regiment would have gone into camp with their full complement.
The hon. gentleman has had a large experience ; will he kindly explain why so many rural corps are dropping out and disbanding ?

I intend explaining it before the close of the session. We have had some experience in the South African war that should be Instructive. For instance I have here the report of the royal commission and I have before me the evidence of Sir Thomas Kelly-Kenny, the present adjutant general of England and one of the best fighting officers in South Africa. Speaking of the pay of the men who went out like the first Canadian contingent and the yeomanry and imperial volunteers of England he says :
Those are what I would call the men who went out through patriotism in the end of 1899 and the beginning of 1900. But as to the other lots the yeomanry and also the other lots of colonials- for I do not think there is very much difference- 421
I think we have had to buy them, and rather dearly.
With the first lot it was not a question of buying and they went through patriotism ; after that it was a question of buying. The pay was raised from one shilling to five shillings and as Sir Thomas Kelly-Kenny says it really meant that they purchased these men for service in South Africa. The volunteer private did not see why he should get only one shilling a day in the volunteer service if he could go out at five shillings a day as a yeoman. The yeoman was receiving five shillings a day without qualification and the service companies one shilling a day for very high qualification. If the strength of volunteer regiments is declining it is owing to a lack of spirit on the part of the officers and non-commissioned officers. I have seen the same thing happen in volunteer regiments years ago. I remember one gentleman marching into camp with a company consisting of six sergeants, one private and himself, when every other company in the regiment had its full complement. Why was this ? Because that gentleman had never taken the trouble to qualify himself or to look after the interests of his company.
As it is almost six o'clock, we might if the committee is agreeable, take a few items and leave an item on which it would be understood we could have a full discussion of all these estimates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I have waited patiently since 11 o'clock this morning in order to make a twenty minute speech and before these items are passed I wish to say something further in reference to this matter.

There are two items under civil government for my department which might be allowed to stand. We might put the others through and permit discussion on all of the items on these two votes.
Mr. I-IACKETT. The best way would be to discuss each item as it comes up. If you desire to adjourn now, I have no objection, but I have listened with much pleasure to the address of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) ; he made a splendid speech and he quoted from a military officer, Sir Thomas Kelly-Kenny. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if Sir Thomas Kelly-Kenny is Irish. There is an item here in connection with an armoury on Prince Edward Island, $500. I would ask the minister if the officers and men) there, loyal and true men, who provided this armoury without any assistance from the government have been reimbursed for their expenditure.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
I have been unable to hear my hon. friend, but if he comes down to the
.REVISED EDITION

front and repeats bis question, I will try and answer it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Between my bad voice and tbe bon. minister's toad ears, it is pretty hard for ns to understand each other. I would like to ask the bon. minister, in regard to this $500 to reimburse the officers and men of Prince Edward Island, how long it is since they paid out their money for this work ?

It was three or four years ago. About three or four years ago the Militia Department was asked for a grant, and it was understood that $500 would be sufficient ; $500 was granted, but the officers were more ambitious and they spent something over $1,000. I took the ground at first that they had no authority to do It, but after carefully looking into the matter and finding that the expenditure was a jn-oper one, I thought it was only fair that they should be reimbursed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: We voted two days ago $2,000 for the same kind of work. These are two votes of the same kind.

There are extensive repairs going on. I understand that this vote is to reimburse the officers for providing an armoury in the drill hall, while the work that is going on now, I think, is an extension of the drill hall, an entirely different thing. This vote is simply to reimburse the officers for money which they paid out, for which we have vouchers in the department, and we are satisfied that the expenditure is bona fide.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Who had charge of the work ?
I could not tell my hon. friend now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: That is very important.
I will give my hon. friend all tlie information. I will undertake to satisfy him.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I suppose there would be no objection to passing this resolution, it being understood that anything in connection with the resolution can be discussed on any other item in the estimates ?

Certainly. There are two items in connection with civil government which will be left, and it will be understood that any question that any hon. member wishes to put in relation to these items may be put, and that I will give an explanation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Or any discussion ?
Certainly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: When will these items be taken up-to-morrow ?
No ; I would prefer to leave them until next week.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: As the items are very short, the hon. minister might let the House have some notice as to when they will be taken up, because there are other hon. gentlemen who would like to continue this discussion and who may not be present if the items are brought up unexpectedly.
If my hon. friend will suggest a day and let me know the day before, I am sure the right hon. leader of the government will be glad to agree to that day.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Very good.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE moved the adjournment of the House.
Would the right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) be good enough to tell us what business we may expect to-morrow ?
Public Works estimates, I think.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at C.10 p.m.
Friday, October 9, 1903.
